w:r.w:t: Are you spending hours on scales and arpeggios, but your solos never sound better?
I certainly did, but a masterclass from Barry Harris changed everything and made it easy to turn exercises into real jazz lines.
in this video, I will show you exactly what Barry taught me and how you can use this exercise to finally play solos that feel and sound like jazz, not just mechanical
This exercise is at the core of Barry’s teaching, yet hardly anyone talks about it. And

Barry often started his masterclass with this exercise.
a practical way to learn the song and connect each chord to the right scale, all in one go.
The basic idea is simple: as you play through the song, you run the scale that matches each chord.
But with a slight twist—I keep the II chord (the m7 chord before the dominant) in the progression. Barry leaves those out.
Let me quickly break down how this works.
the song’s structure, the chord changes, and the scale that fit each chord—all at once.
If a chord lasts one bar (like Gm7 to C7), you play the scale from the root to the 7th note of that scale.
If a chord lasts two bars (like the first two bars), play root up to 7th, then back down to the root again.
This is already super useful. It gives you an overview of the song, so you can easily find your way around the scales and start improvising in one area of the neck.
start with this, then either build a solo by swapping out scales for real solo phrases, or use the exercise to try out a new lick or idea all the way through the song.

Why is the arpeggio from the 3rd so powerful?
The reason the arpeggio from the 3rd is such a great concept is that you are mostly playing the basic chord tones, so for Gmaj7:
The arpeggio is: G B D F#
The 3rd is B, and the diatonic arpeggio on B is Bm7, which gives you B D F# A
you are still playing 3 chord tones, but now add an A on top, which is a beautiful 9th, making your solos more colorful
